title: Personal Statements Are Embarrassing: Here is Mine!
subtitle: And I'm pretty sure with GPT4, they will cease to be written by people...
body_html:
I am a physician. This means I have been forced to write personal statement after personal statement. For medical school applications. For Residency. For Fellowship. And on and on. These are among the least pleasant documents to create, mostly because they live in opposite land:

Personal Statements are anything but personal. They are almost axiomatically written to avoid disclosure of deep personal feelings. Admissions would use those to decide you are too risky for their med school or training program. Despite the abiding and deeply personal motives of people who chose to give their lives to healing others, we ask them to write palatable pablum. Thusly, people won’t judge our scars. And #GPT4 has made writing these things something no one will ever do again.

Here is what I wrote for medical school, with annotations from the present. This was submitted in 2007 and I got accepted to one medical school, my top choice, and then told all the others I was withdrawing my application. I include my current advice to readers on this painful task, assuming you don’t use ChatGPT, as “Comments from the future” in italics, below.

Owen’s Personal Statement to the University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry, written in 2006:

I did not always know I wanted to be a doctor. In fact, I fought the idea.

Comments from the future: always have a hook.

At Amherst, I majored in psychology but intentionally avoided taking pre-med classes, assuming this would be an effective bulwark against the temptation of medical school. I was always interested in the brain and open to the possibility of clinical work, so I thought a psychology Ph.D. would suffice if I chose that path.

Comments from the future: Shorter, declarative sentences. Honestly, I’m already bored with myself.

For a year or so after college, I worked in the music business, which I had been intent on doing since I was a 16-year-old with a 4-track tape machine. Recording engineers, it turns out, are almost exclusively nocturnal. And while I can stay up late with the best of them, that life was not for me. Now, I wondered, what was I going to do with my life?

Comments from the future: this is when you could have mentioned that having bipolar disorder was why profound sleep deprivation was a bad plan. Admit disability to medical school? No way! I’m a radical self-disclosure-ist, but even I still think this is career suicide in an application process.

Soon after leaving Sony Studios, my oldest friend, Alden, had a psychiatric crisis. After two years of physical recovery from a traumatic brain injury, he was struck with severe depression. Every Thursday, for over a year, I went with him to a depression/bipolar support group. I remembered reading in college that group therapy was “effective” for these disorders, but I had no idea what “effective” actually meant. At the group, I got to see healing firsthand and learned how important good psychiatrists were to these patients. I also felt a profound desire to help the people in the group. Alden’s case made it clear to me, however, that a psychology Ph.D. would not suffice. He had a psychiatric disorder, which I understood, and a traumatic brain injury, which I did not. Only as a medical doctor would I be equipped to treat him as a whole person.

Comments from the future: See, there, the lengths I went through to say true-enough things that obscured the deeply personal rationale I had for medical training? This is personal statement gold, people. Fools gold, at least.

That made my decision for me. I enrolled in a post-baccalaureate program and shortly thereafter began volunteering in a children’s psychiatric unit at St. Vincent’s Hospital in Manhattan. This volunteer experience is the hardest and most important thing I do in any given week.

Comments from the future: eh, move it along.

When I walked onto the unit in one of my first weeks there, a young patient was screaming. He continued crying out for the better part of an hour, at which point the art therapist, Martha, informed me that the child was extremely limited by a Pervasive Developmental Disorder. He needed some “one-on-one” attention -- and I would be the one giving it.

I have seldom been so terrified.

Comments from the future: look at how palatable that disclosure is? That is the sweet spot. Vulnerable, appropriately, in an appropriate context, that telegraphs how appropriate everything you've ever felt is.

I armed myself with two puppets and a box of colorful blocks and peeked my head in the door of the less-than-appropriately named “quiet room,” where the patient had been sequestered all morning. Despite my trepidation, I was able to engage the child in a solid 45 minutes of focused play, and both of us were smiling the whole time. When I returned the next week, this same boy made eye contact with me and took my hand, which, I learned, is rare behavior for PDD patients.

Ever since then, I have not had a moment of pause before agreeing to work with any patient, developmental and behavioral disorders notwithstanding. I also have never had a moment of doubt that I should be a doctor, and that I will be a great one.

Thanks for reading. Those who are about to state anything personally, we salute you.

—Owen Scott Muir, M.D.

The frontier psychiatrist is a personal statement for our modern age.
